newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai baht devaluation spurs mild inflation in July.
newsitem.headline: Thai baht devaluation spurs mild inflation in July.

text.p: Thailand's de facto devaluation of the baht caused only mild inflationary pressure in July, official data released on Friday showed.
The Commerce Ministry said the July consumer price index (CPI) rose a moderate 4.9 percent year-on-year against 4.4 percent in June and 5.4 percent a year ago.
Private analysts' expectations for last month's inflation had ranged from 4.6 percent to 5.4 percent.

"We would not see a price explosion in the first month after the baht float as most of its effects would be gradually phased in. Consumer purchasing power remained weak," said Kulthida Malakul of Chao Phaya Finance and Securities Co Ltd.
The baht has depreciated about 23 percent since it was let loose on a new managed float regime on July 2, driving up fuel, utility and consumer product prices.
"The devaluation impact would initially not be so visible partly due to a government price control on basic consumer goods," said Thanawat Pachimkul of Seamico Securities Plc.
A senior ministry official said despite the sharply weaker baht, he did not anticipate inflation to exceed 6.1 percent in the whole of 1997 against 5.9 percent in 1996.
He said the CPI increased only 4.5 percent year-on-year in the first seven months of this year.
The ministry's 1997 inflation forecast was in line with what analysts expected. They expected the CPI to rise an average of 8.0 percent in the second half of 1997.
Thai and foreign financial institutions have predicted that inflation would accelerate to 6.4-9.0 percent in 1998.
The Thai government said it would announce a comprehensive programme to revive the battered Thai economy early next week after consultation with the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
It said the austerity package would likely be backed by an IMF stand-by credit line estimated by the market at $10 billion.

Analysts said the Thai economy would expand only three to four percent this year, its slowest since the early 1960s. That would compare with 6.4 percent gross domestic product growth in 1996 and 8.6 percent a year earlier.

Cash-strapped Thai financial institutions have weathered a crisis of confidence since early this year, largely due to their heavy exposure to the country's ailing property sector which has collapsed after a four-year slump.
Credit ratings agency Standard & Poor's Corp on Friday placed Thailand's "A" long-term foreign currency rating and its "AA" long-term local currency rating on creditwatch with negative implications.

The agency also put eight commercial banks and finance companies, including the largest Thai bank Bangkok Bank Plc, under similar watch due to their poor asset quality, foreign exchange losses, and a slow economic recovery.

It said the move reflected greater than expected loan losses in the financial sector, which were expected to put a sizeable fiscal burden on the government and lead to weakened economic growth for several years.
S&P said its analysts would meet Thai government officials next week to gather more information about the economy.
